title: Level 7 · Advanced Python Coding
blurb: Iterators, generators, decorators, concurrency and the advanced tools professional Python developers use.

lessons.title: Iterators
lessons.concept: An iterator is an object that hands out values one at a time. iter(x) gives you one and next(it) asks for the next value, raising StopIteration when it runs out. Your own class becomes an iterator by defining __iter__ (return self) and __next__.
lessons.why: Every for loop uses iterators behind the scenes, and custom ones let you walk through huge data without loading it all at once.
lessons.example:
it = iter([10, 20])
print(next(it))
print(next(it))
try:
    next(it)
except StopIteration:
    print('done')
lessons.example_note: Pulls two values by hand, then catches the end signal.
lessons.prompt: Write a class Countdown whose constructor takes n. Looping over it must give n, n-1, ... , 1. Define __iter__ and __next__ (raise StopIteration when finished).
hints: __iter__ just returns self.
In __next__, stop with raise StopIteration when current is 0 or less.
Save current in a variable, subtract 1 from self.current, then return the saved value.

lessons.title: Generators
lessons.concept: A generator is a function that uses yield instead of return. Each yield pauses the function and hands out a value; the next request resumes where it stopped. yield from other hands out everything from another iterable.
lessons.why: Generators read big files line by line or produce endless streams while using almost no memory.
lessons.example_note: Prints [1, 2, 'a', 'b'] by chaining generators with yield from.
lessons.prompt: Write a generator function evens(limit) that yields every even number from 0 up to and including limit.
hints: Loop with range and use yield, not return.
range(0, limit + 1, 2) steps by 2.
for n in range(0, limit + 1, 2): yield n

lessons.title: Decorators
lessons.concept: A decorator is a function that takes a function and returns a new, upgraded one. Writing @name above a def is shorthand for f = name(f). Inside, you usually define a wrapper(*args, **kwargs) that calls the original and adds behaviour.
lessons.why: Web frameworks use decorators for routes, logins and caching without touching the original function's code.
lessons.example_note: Prints HI ASHA because the decorator upper-cases the result.
lessons.prompt: Write a decorator double that doubles whatever number the decorated function returns. Apply it with @double to the function add(a, b) already in the starter.
hints: The wrapper calls func(*args, **kwargs) and multiplies the result by 2.
double must return wrapper (not call it).
Add @double on the line directly above def add.

lessons.title: Closures
lessons.concept: A closure is an inner function that remembers variables from the outer function, even after the outer function has finished. To change such a remembered variable (not just read it), declare it with nonlocal.
lessons.why: Closures give you private state without classes: counters, configurable helpers and callbacks all use them.
lessons.example_note: add5 still remembers n = 5 and prints 15.
lessons.prompt: Write make_counter(start) that returns a function. Each call of the returned function adds 1 to the remembered number and returns it, so make_counter(10) gives 11, 12, 13.... Use nonlocal.
lessons.solution:
def make_counter(start):
    count = start
    def counter():
        nonlocal count
        count += 1
        return count
    return counter
hints: Inside counter, write nonlocal count first.
Then count += 1 and return count.
Each make_counter call has its own count, so counters do not interfere.

cases.expr: [c() for c in [make_counter(10)] for _ in range(3)]
(lambda a, b: [a(), a(), b(), a()])(make_counter(0), make_counter(100))

lessons.title: Context Managers
lessons.concept: A context manager is used with with: it runs setup when the block starts and cleanup when it ends, even if an error happens. A class becomes one by defining __enter__ (setup) and __exit__ (cleanup). The contextlib module offers a shortcut with @contextmanager.
lessons.why: Files, database connections and locks all use with so they are always closed or released properly.
lessons.prompt: Write a class Banner with __enter__ printing <<< and __exit__ printing >>>. Then read one line of input and print it inside with Banner():. Input hi prints three lines: <<<, hi, >>>.
lessons.starter:
class Banner:
    # add __enter__ and __exit__
    pass

word = input()
# print word inside a with block
hints: __exit__ takes self, exc_type, exc, tb.
Return self from __enter__ and False from __exit__.
with Banner(): then an indented print(word).

lessons.title: Shallow Copy
lessons.concept: copy.copy(x) makes a shallow copy: a new outer container, but the items inside are still the same objects. So adding to the copy leaves the original alone, yet changing a nested list shows up in both.
lessons.why: Knowing what a copy really shares prevents bugs where changing one list mysteriously changes another.
lessons.example:
import copy
a = [[1], [2]]
b = copy.copy(a)
b.append([3])
b[0].append(99)
print(a)
print(b)
lessons.example_note: a shows the 99 (shared inner list) but not the new [3].
lessons.prompt: Write make_copy(lst) that returns a shallow copy of lst using copy.copy.
lessons.starter:
import copy

def make_copy(lst):
    # return a shallow copy
    return lst
hints: The copy module has a function called copy.
copy.copy(lst) gives a new outer list.
return copy.copy(lst)

lessons.title: Deep Copy
lessons.concept: copy.deepcopy(x) makes a deep copy: it copies the container and everything nested inside, recursively. The result shares nothing with the original, so changes never leak between them. It is slower than a shallow copy, so use it when you really need full independence.
lessons.why: Saving a game state, undo history or a safe copy of a configuration needs a full independent duplicate.
lessons.example:
import copy
a = [[1], [2]]
b = copy.deepcopy(a)
b[0].append(99)
print(a)
print(b)
lessons.prompt: Write clone(data) that returns a deep copy of data using copy.deepcopy.
hints: There is a sibling of copy.copy that goes all the way down.
It is called deepcopy.
return copy.deepcopy(data)

lessons.title: Memory Management
lessons.concept: Variables are references (labels) pointing at objects. a is b asks if two labels point at the same object, while id() shows an object's identity. Python frees an object automatically once nothing refers to it (reference counting, plus a garbage collector for cycles). A weakref points at an object without keeping it alive.
lessons.why: Caches and big programs use weak references so stored objects can still be freed when nobody else needs them.
lessons.example:
import weakref

class Box:
    pass

b = Box()
r = weakref.ref(b)
print(r() is b)
del b
print(r())
lessons.example_note: Prints True, then None because the Box was freed.
lessons.prompt: In the starter, Node has a name. Write weak_demo(name): create a Node(name), make a weakref.ref to it, record the node's name through the reference, then del the node. Return a tuple (recorded_name, ref() is None).
hints: ref = weakref.ref(node) ; calling ref() gives the object (or None).
Save ref().name in a variable before deleting.
After del node, ref() is None, so return (seen, ref() is None).

lessons.title: GIL
lessons.concept: CPython has a Global Interpreter Lock (GIL): only one thread runs Python bytecode at a time. Threads therefore do not speed up heavy maths, but they are great for waiting on files or networks. The GIL does not make count += 1 safe: that is several steps, so threads can interleave. Protect shared data with a threading.Lock.
lessons.why: Understanding the GIL tells you when to pick threads (waiting work) and when to pick processes (number crunching).
lessons.example_note: Prints 4000 every time because the lock guards the shared counter.
lessons.prompt: Write safe_count(threads, per_thread): start threads threads, each adding 1 to a shared counter per_thread times while holding a Lock. Wait for all with join() and return the total.
lessons.starter:
import threading

def safe_count(threads, per_thread):
    # shared counter + Lock + threads
    return 0
hints: Keep the counter in a list like [0] so the inner function can change it.
Use with lock: around the increment.
Start all threads first, then join them all, then return total[0].

lessons.title: Multithreading
lessons.concept: The threading module runs functions in several threads: Thread(target=f, args=(x,)), then .start() and .join() to wait. A common safe pattern is to give each thread its own slot in a list to write into, and use a Lock for anything shared such as a total.
lessons.why: Downloading many web pages or reading many files at once is much faster with threads, since they spend their time waiting.
lessons.example_note: Each thread fills its own slot, printing [0, 10, 20].
lessons.prompt: Write threaded_squares(nums): start one thread per number. Each thread stores its square in its own index of a result list and also adds it to a shared total under a Lock. Return (squares_list, total).
hints: Pre-build squares = [0] * len(nums) so each thread owns one index.
Pass the index and number with args=(i, n).
Start every thread, join every thread, then return (squares, total[0]).

lessons.title: Multiprocessing
lessons.concept: A process is a separate Python with its own memory and its own GIL, so several processes can crunch numbers truly in parallel. With multiprocessing.Pool(4).map(func, chunks) (or Process) you hand each worker a piece of the data. Before fanning out you must split the work into chunks. (Our practice sandbox cannot start processes, so you will write the splitting helper.)
lessons.why: Image processing, simulations and data crunching use one process per CPU core to finish several times faster.
lessons.example:
data = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7]
q, r = divmod(len(data), 3)
print(q, r)
# 7 items over 3 workers: sizes 3, 2, 2
lessons.example_note: divmod gives the base chunk size and how many chunks get one extra item.
lessons.prompt: Write split_chunks(items, n) that returns a list of n lists in order, as equal as possible, with the earlier chunks getting the extra items. split_chunks([1,2,3,4,5,6,7], 3) is [[1,2,3],[4,5],[6,7]]. If there are fewer items than n, the last chunks are empty.
hints: size, extra = divmod(len(items), n): every chunk gets size, the first extra chunks get one more.
Keep a start index and slice items[start:end] for each chunk.
end = start + size + (1 if i < extra else 0)

lessons.title: Async Programming
lessons.concept: Async code lets one thread juggle many waiting tasks. Define a coroutine with async def, pause for results with await, run many at once with asyncio.gather(...), and start the whole thing from normal code with asyncio.run(...). Results from gather come back in the order you gave them.
lessons.why: Web servers and chat apps use async to serve thousands of users at once while waiting on networks and databases.
lessons.example:
import asyncio

async def square(x):
    await asyncio.sleep(0)
    return x * x

async def main():
    return await asyncio.gather(square(2), square(3))

print(asyncio.run(main()))
lessons.prompt: Write async def double(x) that does await asyncio.sleep(0) and returns x * 2. Then write a normal function run_all(nums) that uses asyncio.gather inside an async helper and asyncio.run to return the list of doubled numbers.
lessons.starter:
import asyncio

# write async def double(x)

def run_all(nums):
    # an async main() using gather, started with asyncio.run
    return []
hints: gather(*coroutines) takes the coroutines as separate arguments.
Define async def main() inside run_all and await gather in it.
return asyncio.run(main())

lessons.title: Metaclasses
lessons.concept: Classes are objects too, and a metaclass is the class that builds them (by default it is type). Subclass type and override __new__(mcs, name, bases, attrs) to change a class's attributes while it is being created, then use it with class X(metaclass=Meta).
lessons.why: Frameworks such as Django models and ORMs use metaclasses to inspect and rewrite your class definitions automatically.
lessons.example_note: The metaclass added kind to Thing; prints tagged.
lessons.prompt: Write a metaclass Shout that renames every attribute whose name does not start with __ to UPPERCASE. Then define class Config(metaclass=Shout) with host = 'local' and port = 80, so Config.HOST is 'local'.
hints: Loop over attrs.items() and make a new dict.
Keep keys starting with __ unchanged, uppercase the rest.
Pass the new dict to super().__new__(mcs, name, bases, new).

cases.expr: sorted(k for k in vars(Config) if not k.startswith('__'))

lessons.title: Descriptors
lessons.concept: A descriptor is an object stored on a class that controls how an attribute is read and written. It defines __get__(self, obj, objtype) and/or __set__(self, obj, value), and optionally __set_name__(self, owner, name) to learn the attribute name. Properties are built from descriptors.
lessons.why: Reusable validation (positive numbers, non-empty text) across many fields is done with one descriptor class.
lessons.example_note: Reading a.x calls Loud.__get__ and prints LOUD.
lessons.prompt: Write a descriptor class Clamp with __set_name__, __get__ and __set__ that stores each instance's value (in '_' + name) but turns negative numbers into 0. Product is already in the starter and uses it for price.
hints: __set_name__ saves '_' + name on the descriptor.
__get__ returns getattr(obj, self.name, 0); __set__ uses setattr.
In __set__, store max(0, value).

lessons.title: Type Hints
lessons.concept: Type hints label what types a function expects and returns: def area(w: float, h: float) -> float:. Python does not enforce them, but editors and tools like mypy use them to catch mistakes. They are stored in the function's __annotations__. Modern Python writes generics like list[int] and dict[str, int].
lessons.why: Large teams use type hints so code documents itself and bugs are found before the program ever runs.
lessons.example:
def area(w: float, h: float) -> float:
    return w * h

print(area(2.0, 3.0))
print(area.__annotations__)
lessons.example_note: Prints 6.0 and the dictionary of hints.
lessons.prompt: Write average(nums: list[float]) -> float that returns the mean of the list, or 0.0 for an empty list. Keep the type hints exactly as shown.
hints: Write nums: list[float] for the parameter and -> float after the parentheses.
Check for an empty list first.
return sum(nums) / len(nums)

lessons.title: Dataclasses
lessons.concept: @dataclass (from dataclasses) writes the boring parts of a class for you. List fields with type hints and it creates __init__, a readable __repr__ and ==. Fields can have defaults, and you can still add normal methods.
lessons.why: Dataclasses are the tidy way to model records such as users, orders and settings in modern Python.
lessons.example:
from dataclasses import dataclass

@dataclass
class Point:
    x: int
    y: int = 0

print(Point(3))
print(Point(1, 2) == Point(1, 2))
lessons.example_note: Prints Point(x=3, y=0) and True, all without writing __init__.
lessons.prompt: Create a dataclass Item with fields name: str, price: float and qty: int = 1, plus a method total() returning price * qty.
lessons.starter:
from dataclasses import dataclass

# write the Item dataclass
hints: Put @dataclass on the line above class Item.
Fields look like name: str, and the default is qty: int = 1.
def total(self): return self.price * self.qty

lessons.title: Collections (Counter, deque, defaultdict)
lessons.concept: The collections module has handy containers. Counter counts items, deque is a list that is fast to add or remove at both ends, and defaultdict creates a missing key's value automatically (for example defaultdict(list)). Counter(...).most_common(n) returns the top n as (item, count) pairs.
lessons.why: Word counts, queues of tasks and grouping records by category are everyday jobs these containers make short.
lessons.example:
from collections import Counter, deque, defaultdict
print(Counter('banana').most_common(2))
q = deque([1, 2, 3]); q.appendleft(0); print(list(q))
g = defaultdict(list); g['a'].append(1); print(dict(g))
lessons.example_note: Counts letters, adds to the front of a deque, and groups with defaultdict.
lessons.prompt: Write top_words(text, n) that lowercases the text, splits it on spaces and returns the n most common words as a list of (word, count) pairs using Counter.
lessons.starter:
from collections import Counter

def top_words(text, n):
    # count the lowercase words
    return []
hints: text.lower().split() gives the list of words.
Counter(words) counts them.
return Counter(text.lower().split()).most_common(n)

cases.expr: top_words('the cat and The dog and the bird', 2)

lessons.title: Functional Programming
lessons.concept: Functional style favours pure functions: the output depends only on the inputs, and nothing outside is changed (no side effects). It also favours immutability: instead of modifying data, build a new value. Tools such as map, filter and tuple help.
lessons.why: Pure functions are easy to test, safe to run in parallel threads and simple to reason about.
lessons.example:
def with_tax(prices, rate):
    return [round(p * (1 + rate), 2) for p in prices]

prices = (100, 200)
print(with_tax(prices, 0.1))
print(prices)
lessons.example_note: Returns new prices and leaves the original untouched.
lessons.prompt: Write a pure function add_item(cart, item) that returns a new list with item added at the end, without changing cart. Do not use append or extend.
hints: Mutating methods like append change the original.
The + operator on lists builds a new list.
return cart + [item]
